rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined about what is known, what is missing, and what should not be pitched yet. Its strongest line, “Toast doesn’t say how often its restaurant cash advances go bad,” turns a supplied disclosure gap into an actual accountability story. B has real shape, but “Restaurants are borrowing from their point-of-sale system instead of their bank” overreaches into bank displacement and underwriting mechanics the update does not prove.
gaps_in_A: “Toast's profits are coming from lending and payroll” is a hair stronger than the facts allow; the update says lending and fintech are higher-margin and Toast recently reached profitability, not that profits are definitively coming from those products.
The payroll angle is serviceable but thin: “betting restaurants haven't solved their tipped-and-hourly wage math” needs product detail before it becomes more than a trade-product brief.
“Decay: 24hr” on the payroll launch is too mechanical when the update does not establish an actual launch date or announcement source.
gaps_in_B: “instead of their bank” invents a displacement frame. The facts say Toast offers cash advances, not that restaurants are replacing bank credit or that community banks are losing borrowers.
“underwritten by the payment flow Toast already sees” is a plausible inference, but still an inference; the update only says advances are repaid as a share of daily sales.

“Tipped wages, split shifts, and the payroll problem restaurant software keeps dodging” adds color the facts do not supply. Tipped and hourly staff are in the update; split shifts, tip pooling, wage credits, and dodging are not.

Refusing “Toast responds to fee criticism” as `no_why_now_but_required` is too timid. Bundling more financial products while owners complain about fees is exactly the live tension a trade reporter could use.
